*Four consecutive earnings calls reviewed: Half-Year 2024 (Jul 2024), Full-Year 2024 (Feb 2025), Half-Year 2025 (Jul 2025), and Full-Year 2025 (Feb 2026). Cross-referenced against the screener's financial trajectory and live-verified facts as of late June 2026, including the Q1 2026 trading update (May 2026).*

Wolters Kluwer is a Dutch professional-information and software company. It sells subscriptions, cloud software, and expert tools to lawyers, tax-and-accounting firms, doctors and nurses, and corporate-compliance teams across five divisions — Health, Tax & Accounting, Financial & Corporate Compliance, Legal & Regulatory, and Corporate Performance & ESG. About 83% of revenue is recurring, and roughly 70% of its digital revenue now comes from products it describes as "AI-powered." One important note for the reader: the screener files this company under "Industrials," but in substance it is a subscription data-and-software business, so the right comparison set is information-services peers (RELX, Thomson Reuters, Verisk, S&P Global), not industrial manufacturers.

A second, critical note on price. The screener's headline says "Fair Value 130.7 / Margin of Safety 148%" and "3% up the 52-week range," which makes the stock look as if it has crashed to a fraction of fair value. The market price of about €57 is real and current — but the stock has *de-rated*, not collapsed on broken fundamentals. It is down roughly 35% so far this year and far more from its 2024 peak, on a specific fear (artificial-intelligence disruption of professional information), while the business itself kept growing. The €131 "fair value" is the screener's intrinsic model output; the live analyst consensus target is closer to €100, and that is the more defensible upside anchor.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across these four calls the story is remarkably steady and, if anything, *strengthening operationally* — which is the opposite of the share price. This is the central tension of the file.

- **Half-Year 2024** set the template: 6% organic growth (revenue growth excluding currency swings and acquisitions/disposals), an improving adjusted operating margin (26.5%), and diluted adjusted earnings per share up 11% in constant currencies. Management framed the company as a steady compounder shifting toward "expert solutions" (its higher-value software products), which had reached 59% of revenue, with recurring cloud software growing 16% organically.
- **Full-Year 2024** confirmed the pattern: 6% organic growth, margin up 70 basis points to 27.1%, earnings per share up 11%, free cash flow up 9%, return on invested capital (the profit earned on the money put into the business) of 18.1%, and a €1 billion buyback. Management also flagged the CEO succession — Nancy McKinstry handing to Stacey Caywood.
- **Half-Year 2025** showed the AI strategy moving from talk to product: recurring cloud software up 15% organically, generative-AI features rolling out, and the first agentic-AI products promised for later in the year. The company leaned harder into mid-market software with three acquisitions (RASi, Brightflag, Libra) and divested a small unit (FRR) for nearly €400 million. Margin jumped 190 basis points to 28.4%.
- **Full-Year 2025** (Feb 2026) was the most confident on the franchise: 6% organic growth, margin up to 27.5% (top of guidance), free cash flow over €1.3 billion (+10%), and — the headline tell — "nearly 70% of our digital revenues are from AI-powered solutions." Management positioned AI as a tailwind it is monetizing (UpToDate Expert AI, CCH Axcess Expert AI), not a threat eroding it. The 2026 outlook, reaffirmed in May, calls for another year of good organic growth, ~28% margin, and high-single-digit earnings-per-share growth.

The growth driver introduced and amplified over the period is generative and agentic AI as a *product*, framed as a productivity upsell. Nothing material was quietly dropped; the narrative is unusually consistent.

| Management claim | The actual numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Steady ~6% organic growth | Revenue €5.45B (2022) → €5.58B → €5.92B → €6.12B (2025); ~3.5–4% reported, 6% organic ex-FX/M&A; Q1 2026 +5% organic | Verified. Organic growth has been genuinely steady at 5–6% for years. |

The narrative is, unusually, *neither richer nor poorer* than the numbers — it matches them closely. **Stable-to-Rising.** The tone is consistent and businesslike throughout, and it grows *more* confident on AI as the period progresses — the reverse of a company on the defensive.

- Half-Year 2024: "good start to the year… on track to meet our full year guidance."
- Full-Year 2024: "another year of 6% organic growth… a good year."
- Half-Year 2025: "solid start… diluted adjusted EPS rose 14% in constant currencies."
- Full-Year 2025: "nearly 70% of our digital revenues are from AI-powered solutions… we made significant progress on our AI strategy." Incoming CEO Stacey Caywood: "excited to build on our momentum and to accelerate our strategy."

Guidance has stayed specific (margin ranges, EPS-growth ranges, cash-conversion targets) and was even *raised* mid-2025. There is no drift from offense to defense in management's own words.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High.** The screener shows an 86% beat rate (6 of 7 quarters), and the calls repeatedly land within or above guided ranges — Full-Year 2024 margin came in *above* the guided range, Full-Year 2025 margin hit the *top* of the range, and 2025 earnings-per-share guidance was raised in July and then delivered. Cash-conversion guidance (95–100%) was beaten (102–103%) on year-end collections. There is no egregious sandbagging tell; guidance is set realistically and met. Management is candid about soft spots (transactional revenue weakness in compliance from subdued mergers and lending; print-book decline of 11–17%), which adds to credibility.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **AI disruption / monetization.** This is the dominant and recurring question (Half-Year 2025, Full-Year 2025). Lisa Yang of Goldman Sachs pressed directly on whether management could *quantify* the AI benefit; management conceded "it's early days right now in terms of doing that" — supportive of retention and price increases, but not yet a hard number. That inability to quantify is precisely the gap the market is exploiting on the downside.
- **Pricing power under AI.** Analysts probed value-based pricing; management's answer (price-to-value, multiple metrics, Libra priced at "about 2x the content offering") is detailed and credible but, again, not yet proven in disclosed numbers.
- **M&A intensity versus the buyback.** With ~€1.7B of acquisitions in 2025, analysts asked whether deal spend would crowd out buybacks. Management held the line on capital-allocation priorities, but the 2026 buyback was in fact cut to €500M (from €1B) — a real, if undiscussed-on-call, downshift.
- **ESG/regulatory pullback.** A pointed question on whether the ESG-reporting backlash would hurt the Corporate Performance & ESG division; management argued the software is operational, not just compliance, and the division kept growing 7%.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 The single existential question — does generative AI let professionals self-serve the curated legal/tax/medical answers they used to pay Wolters Kluwer for? — cannot be answered from the filings, only with management reassurance. This is the same unfalsifiable claim that is repricing the entire professional-information cohort.

🔴 Non-recurring revenue (on-premise licenses, implementation, print books) is in structural decline (−5% organic in 2025, print down double digits), a persistent ~15% drag on the mix.

🔴 The 2026 buyback was halved to €500M versus €1B in 2025 — the per-share-value engine slowed even as the stock got cheaper, the opposite of what an opportunistic allocator would do at a depressed price.

🟢 Organic growth (5–6%), margins (rising to 27.5%), return on invested capital (~18%), and free cash flow (+10%, over €1.3B) are all *stable to improving* — there is no operational deterioration to corroborate the share-price fear.

🟢 The business is genuinely sticky: 83% recurring revenue, multiyear enterprise contracts with high renewals, gross retention in UpToDate in the "low 90s," and longer-duration, higher-value contracts signed in 2025 than in prior years.

🟢 Management is monetizing AI from a position of proprietary content (UpToDate Expert AI, CCH Axcess Expert AI), with editorial verification on top — the part of the moat hardest for a general-purpose model to replicate.

🟢 Smooth, internal CEO succession to a "proven Wolters Kluwer leader," with no strategy reset.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The repeated framing "70% of digital revenue is AI-powered" is a deliberate counter-narrative: management is pre-empting the disruption fear by recasting AI as *its own* product. Whether the market believes it is the whole debate.
- The shift toward mid-market software (RASi, Brightflag, Libra) and away from mature, transaction-heavy enterprise legal management is a quiet repositioning toward faster-growing, more-recurring segments.
- The buyback downshift to €500M while spending €1.7B on acquisitions signals management would rather *buy growth* than buy back its own depressed stock — a defensible long-term choice, but a missed opportunity if the AI fear proves overblown.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE — a high-quality compounder priced for a decline that its own numbers do not yet show.** The operating business is doing everything right: steady organic growth, rising margins, strong and growing cash flow, stable high returns, and an AI strategy that (so far) reads as monetization rather than cannibalization. The drawdown is a *fear-print* on a forward secular worry, not a response to any fundamental crack.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing:** whether the AI-displacement fear is a temporary mispricing (the bull case — proprietary, verified, liability-grade professional content is not replaceable by a general model, and the stock is cheap on a quality franchise) or the leading edge of a genuine secular impairment of the franchise's pricing power and retention (the bear case). This is the *same* unresolved, cohort-wide driver hammering RELX, Thomson Reuters, and Gartner at the same time — so the cheapness versus those peers is largely shared sector beta, not Wolters-Kluwer-specific edge. Everything turns on this one question, and it cannot be settled from the filings.

**Moat:** intangible-brand plus switching-costs — proprietary, editorially-verified content (UpToDate, CCH Axcess, VitalLaw), deeply embedded in professional workflows, sold on multiyear contracts with high renewals. By the returns-and-margin evidence the moat is **NARROW** and **STABLE**: return on invested capital has held at ~18% and margins are *rising*, not falling, so this is not a classic melting-margin erosion. An independent rater (Morningstar) cut the moat to "narrow" specifically on AI-disruption potential, which is why "narrow" rather than "wide" is the honest call despite the strong financials. **Secular threat: material, not terminal.** Generative AI is a real structural risk to a "we sell you curated knowledge" business, and it is the explicit reason for the de-rating — but the proprietary primary content, the liability-grade verification professionals require, and the embedded multiyear contracts are not trivially replicated, and there is no evidence yet (only the fear) of actual displacement in the numbers. The drawdown looks more like a fear-print on a still-growing base than confirmation of a shrinking one — but the secular tail is real enough to cap how aggressive one should be on the value case.

There is a mild, systematic conservatism (sandbagging) in how they set the bar — useful to know, because it means the standing 2026 guide is more likely a floor than a stretch. Nothing in the record suggests guidance you cannot trust.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The recurring pressure is exactly the market's fear: can AI monetization be *proven*, and is UpToDate (the crown-jewel clinical reference) safe? Analysts pushed repeatedly on quantifying the AI benefit and on health-division growth quality (Goldman's Lisa Yang, Deutsche's Silvia Cuneo, ING's Thymen Rundberg). Management's answers are qualitative — "supports retention... supports price increases" — and they decline to disclose UpToDate's precise gross retention or the growth rate of acquired units. That non-answer is the seam the bears are prying at. A specific external data point outside the transcripts sharpens it: at least one sell-side analysis projects UpToDate to shift to *negative* growth over the medium term on customer churn and pricing pressure. Management's counter is that they signed "more multiyear contracts for longer durations with higher annual contract value" in 2025 — a direct rebuttal, but one investors are choosing not to believe yet.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Green: Returns and margins are flat-to-rising (ROIC ~18%, margin to 27.5%) — the empirical signature of an intact moat, not an eroding one.
- Green: 83% recurring revenue, ~7% recurring growth, and a self-funding ~EUR 1B/yr buyback that at today's depressed price retires roughly 7% of the shares annually — highly accretive if the business is worth anything like its history.
- Green: Consistent guidance delivery and an orderly, long-signaled CEO succession.
- Red (soft): The non-recurring lines (print down 11%, on-premise licenses down 5-10%) are in structural decline; management frames this as a mix choice, but it is the first place any AI substitution would show, and it is negative now.
- Red (soft): The load-bearing forward claim — AI as a monetization tailwind — is explicitly "not yet quantifiable." Investors are asked to take it on trust while the multiple says they don't.
- Red (governance-lite): Acquisition spend stepped up to ~EUR 900M/yr; leverage touched 2.1x. Well within tolerance, but worth watching if growth slows.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling terminology shift is from "gen-AI features" (an add-on) to "AI-powered solutions are ~70% of digital revenue" and "Agentic AI" (the core) — management is deliberately reframing AI from threat to substrate. The pricing language also hardened: the new CEO leans into "price to value" and cites Libra at "2x the content offering," signalling an intent to *capture* AI value rather than merely defend. On competition, note what is *absent*: no mention of losing customers to AI-native rivals, and repeated emphasis that their models are "small language models... only our proprietary content" with "editorial resources on top" — the authority-and-liability defense (a doctor or lawyer needs a citable, verified answer, not a plausible one). Finally, the divestment of FRR (~EUR 400M) alongside tuck-in buys of faster-growing SaaS (Brightflag, Libra, Isabel/Codabox) shows an active hand rotating the portfolio toward the AI-resistant, workflow-embedded end.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** This is a well-run, cash-generative, wide-moat compounder executing consistently while its stock is repriced for a future that has not arrived in the numbers. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **this is a bet on the durability of the moat against generative-AI substitution, and that bet is not resolution-independent** — it rides the single most crowded fear in the market (AI displacing knowledge-work software). The evidence (flat-to-rising returns, 6% organic growth, monetizing AI) says the fear is over-extrapolated across a franchise that is really five businesses — two of which (tax-and-accounting compliance software, corporate-performance/ESG software) are barely AI-substitutable, one of which (corporate compliance / registered-agent) is a regulatory moat, and only two of which (health reference, standalone legal research) carry real substitution risk. But the market can stay fearful longer than a value buyer can stay solvent, and there is no hard catalyst to force the re-rating.

**Moat: WIDE, switching-costs + intangible-brand + regulatory-embedding.** Evidence: ROIC ~18% and stable, gross margin 73.5%, operating margin rising to 27.5%, 83% recurring revenue, decades-long customer relationships with high renewal rates. **Moat trend: STABLE** — returns are not falling, so the moat is not (yet) eroding on the numbers; margins are rising while ROIC holds flat as acquisitions dilute incremental returns. **Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal** — generative AI is a genuine long-horizon cap on pricing power for the "good-enough answer" tier (medical reference, legal research), but WKL's proprietary, liability-grade, workflow-embedded content is a real defense and is currently monetizing AI, not being displaced by it. The cheapness is therefore best read as a fear-print on a durable base with a real but partial risk — closer to a mispricing than a value trap, provided the recurring lines and UpToDate retention hold. The next two half-year prints (late July 2026, February 2027) are the evidence that will settle it.

The first hard evidence arrived in the first quarter of 2026, the first full quarter after Anthropic launched its legal plug-in for Claude on 3 February 2026 and took roughly a tenth off this share price in a day. Every division still grew: health 5%, tax and accounting 4%, financial and corporate compliance 5%, legal and regulatory 5%, corporate performance and environmental, social and governance 5%. The division the bears named did not decelerate. Guidance was reaffirmed at the same update. The second piece of evidence arrived on 23 July 2026 when RELX, the closest comparable business in the world, reported underlying revenue up 7% with growth accelerating in its legal division and reaffirmed its outlook.

There is also a case that artificial intelligence is a revenue opportunity here rather than only a threat. Management disclosed in February 2026 that Libra, its legal workspace product, is priced at roughly twice the content offering it would otherwise sell a law firm, and that more than half of United States enterprise customers have adopted UpToDate Expert AI, with over 150 accounting firms on the new agentic modules in CCH Axcess. A company whose product is being displaced does not raise price by a factor of two.

Finally, the capital return is substantial and the balance sheet is sound. Dividends and buybacks totalled 1.7 billion euros in 2025, more than 120% of free cash flow. Leverage is 1.9 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation as of March 2026, comfortably inside the company's 1.5 to 2.5 times target range, with the Altman-Z solvency score at 3.2 in the safe zone. For the bull case to work, nothing heroic is required: the group simply has to keep growing at 4-6% with a stable margin for another few reporting periods while the market gradually accepts that the profit pool at risk is a tenth, not a half.
bear_thesis:
The bear case does not require Wolters Kluwer to collapse. It only requires the market to be right that the terminal value of a professional-information franchise is permanently lower in a world of capable language models, in which case today's multiple is not a bargain but a fair price for a slowly-decaying annuity.

Start with what is genuinely deteriorating. Roughly 17% of revenue is already shrinking. Non-recurring revenue fell 4% organically in the first half of 2025, with the on-premise licence and implementation component down 9%. Print books fell 11% across the group and 17% within health in the same period, and print alone cost the group 50 basis points of organic growth in 2025. Financial and corporate compliance decelerated to 3% organic growth in 2025 on subdued deal and lending volumes and the suspended enforcement of the Corporate Transparency Act. The headline 5-6% is therefore being carried by a narrowing base, and organic growth has in fact stepped down from 6% to 5% in the most recent quarter.

Second, the cost of defending the franchise is rising, permanently. Management guided product development spending up from a stable 11% of revenue to 12-13% in 2026 explicitly to advance the artificial-intelligence strategy. On a 6.1 billion euro revenue base that is roughly 60 to 120 million euros of additional annual cost, and there is no reason to think it reverses. This is the clearest concession in the file that the competitive bar has risen, and it arrives at the same moment as a margin the screener flags as 1.34 standard deviations above its historical peak. A company simultaneously at peak margin and stepping up permanent spending is not a company with room for error.

Third, and most damaging, management will not produce the three numbers that would settle the argument. Asked directly by Goldman Sachs in July 2025 to quantify the benefit of artificial intelligence, the answer was that it is early days and they are still working through it. Asked in the same call for the growth rates of Isabel, RASi and Brightflag, the answer was an explicit refusal. Asked in February 2026 for UpToDate's gross retention rate, with the analyst helpfully offering low nineties as a starting point, the answer was qualitative. Nearly 1.25 billion euros of acquisitions across 2024 and 2025 are described as performing ahead of expectations with no supporting figures. When a company that has been asked the same question for four consecutive quarters still cannot answer it, the reasonable inference is that the answer is not yet flattering.

Fourth, the capital-allocation posture has loosened. The company paid nine to ten times sales for the Isabel accounting assets against a historical five to six times, a change an analyst flagged in real time in July 2024. Acquisition spending then reached 896 million euros in 2025 and leverage rose from 1.6 to 2.1 times within twelve months. Meanwhile the 2026 buyback is set at up to 500 million euros against 1,096 million euros actually deployed in 2025, removing a meaningful part of the mechanical bid under the shares at precisely the moment sentiment is weakest.

Fifth, there is no floor. Intangible assets are roughly 69% of total assets, tangible book value is deeply negative, and net debt is 4.2 billion euros including capitalised leases. If the earnings power is impaired there is nothing underneath the equity to catch it. The screener's own model spread reflects this disagreement honestly: discounted cash flow, Graham and owner-earnings methods all point 50-62% higher, but earnings-power value sits 60% below the price and the 15%-required-return method sits 92% below, because those methods refuse to capitalise growth and charge the full debt load.

What would confirm the bear case: organic growth printing below 4% at the 5 August 2026 half-year results, particularly if legal and regulatory decelerates; any downgrade to the roughly 28.0% margin target; product development spending drifting above 13%; or a renewal cycle in which UpToDate or CCH Axcess pricing has to be conceded to hold volume. The most likely path to being wrong here is not a crash but a slow, grinding compression in which the company keeps reporting 4-5% growth, keeps spending more to get it, and simply never re-rates.
consensus_delta:
The street is pricing a terminal decline into a company whose earnings power has not declined in any reporting period yet, and the specific assumption that is factually wrong is the size of the exposed profit pool.

The market's implied view, readable in a share price 53% below its 52-week high and an 11.9 times earnings multiple, is that generative artificial intelligence commoditises what Wolters Kluwer sells. That is treated as a statement about the company. It is actually a statement about one division. Legal and regulatory generated 1,005 million euros of revenue and 183 million euros of adjusted operating profit in 2025: 16% of group revenue but only about 10% of divisional profit, at the lowest margin in the group (18.2%). Everything else is protected by something other than content. CT Corporation inside financial and corporate compliance (437 million euros of profit, 35.2% margin) exists because United States law requires every registered entity to appoint a registered agent, which no language model changes. Tax and accounting (584 million euros, 35.2%) sells filing engines wired into firm calendars and is a net beneficiary of spreading European electronic-invoicing mandates. Health (512 million euros, 32.1%) is UpToDate, whose value is precisely that a human editorial layer and the associated professional liability stand behind the answer at the point of clinical decision. A reasonable estimate is that the market is pricing perhaps a third to a half of the profit pool as impaired when the defensible figure is about a tenth.

The second wrong assumption is that this is a forecast rather than a testable claim, and it has now been tested twice. The first quarter of 2026 was the first full quarter after Anthropic's 3 February 2026 legal plug-in launch, the event that took roughly a tenth off this share price in a single session. In that quarter every division grew: health 5%, tax and accounting 4%, financial and corporate compliance 5%, legal and regulatory 5%, corporate performance and environmental, social and governance 5%. The division the bears named specifically did not decelerate at all. Then on 23 July 2026 RELX, the closest comparable business in the world, reported underlying revenue up 7% with adjusted operating profit up 9% and margin up to 35.5%, and described growth as accelerating in its scientific and legal divisions. Deutsche Bank's note the following day was headed with the judgement that artificial-intelligence worries look overplayed.

The third wrong assumption is directional: that artificial intelligence subtracts from price. The disclosed evidence says the opposite so far. Libra, the legal workspace product, is priced at roughly twice the content offering the company would otherwise sell a law firm. More than half of United States enterprise customers have taken UpToDate Expert AI and over 150 accounting firms are on the new agentic modules in CCH Axcess. Management is charging for the technology that is supposed to be destroying it.

Where the street is right, and where this committee does not disagree: the old premium multiple is not coming back, the risk is permanent rather than cyclical, and the company has refused for four consecutive quarters to quantify artificial-intelligence revenue, acquisition growth rates or UpToDate retention. The disagreement is about magnitude, not direction. The market has repriced a tenth of the profit pool as though it were the whole company.
forcing_function:
The re-rating is not waiting on a single event; it is being forced by a sequence of scheduled results prints that repeatedly fail to show the damage the market has priced. Two of them have already fired. The first quarter 2026 trading update on 6 May 2026 showed all five divisions growing 4-5% in the first full quarter after the 3 February 2026 Anthropic legal plug-in launch, with guidance reaffirmed. The second, and the reason this call changes today, was RELX's half-year results on 23 July 2026: underlying revenue up 7%, adjusted operating profit up 9% to 1.7 billion pounds, margin up to 35.5% from 34.8%, outlook reaffirmed, and growth accelerating in the legal division specifically. That print moved this share price roughly 12.7% in three sessions and produced sell-side capitulation on the bear thesis, with Deutsche Bank writing that artificial-intelligence worries look overplayed and lifting its target, and UBS reiterating a target implying roughly 47% upside for RELX.

The next hard date is Wolters Kluwer's own half-year 2026 results on 5 August 2026, nine days away. This is the decisive one because it converts read-across into own-company evidence. The specific things that force the re-rating: organic growth at or above 5%, the roughly 28.0% full-year margin target reaffirmed, and above all the legal and regulatory division holding near 5%. A fourth item would be more valuable than all of them, and management has been asked for it four quarters running: a quantified figure for revenue attributable to artificial-intelligence products. Any disclosure that puts a number on the Libra pricing uplift or UpToDate Expert AI monetisation would remove the central unfalsifiable element of the bear case in one step.

After that the calendar runs to the interim dividend ex-date on 1 September 2026, a nine-month trading update on 4 November 2026, and full-year 2026 results with 2027 guidance on 24 February 2027. That February date carries additional weight as the first full-year guidance from the new chief executive and the point at which the elevated 12-13% product development spending is either confirmed as a permanent new base or framed as an investment peak.

A secondary, less predictable forcing function is corporate. This is a family-influenced Dutch company with a wide moat, negative tangible book and no controlling takeover defence being tested, trading at roughly half the earnings multiple of its closest peer. At 15.2 billion euros of market value with 8.9% free-cash-flow yield it is now a plausible target for a strategic or large-scale private capital approach, and the current regime read describes a record first half for global deal announcements with financing wide open. That is optionality rather than a thesis, and it is not being underwritten here.
valley_of_death:
There is no financing cliff here, which is the first thing to establish. Leverage was 1.9 times cash profit at 31 March 2026, inside the company's 1.5 to 2.5 times target range; the Altman-Z solvency score is 3.2, in the safe zone; interest cover is roughly nineteen times (86 million euros of adjusted net financing costs against 1,687 million euros of adjusted operating profit); and guided 2026 free cash flow of 1,300 to 1,350 million euros comfortably funds the dividend and the buyback. The risky window over the next three to nine months is about evidence and sentiment, not solvency.

The sharpest near-term risk is the 5 August 2026 half-year results, nine days away, taken immediately after a roughly 12.7% three-session rally. The bar has just been raised by the tape itself. Organic growth printing below 4%, any softening of the roughly 28.0% margin target, or a visible deceleration in legal and regulatory would hand the bears their first piece of hard confirming evidence and would likely retrace the entire move; a retest of the 54.64 euro 52-week low is a realistic outcome, roughly 19% below the current price. There is also a specific known drag in the second half: management flagged in July 2025 that currency headwinds and additional restructuring weigh on the back half, and the 2026 numbers absorb the step-up in product development spending to 12-13% of revenue, which is a genuine margin headwind arriving in exactly this window.

Second, the composition risk. Roughly 17% of revenue is already shrinking and will keep shrinking through this period: print books were down 11% group-wide and 17% in health in the first half of 2025, and on-premise licences and implementation revenue fell 9% organically. If the recurring base slows even slightly while these keep declining, the headline can break below 4% for reasons that have nothing to do with artificial intelligence but will be read as though they do.

Third, the transactional exposure. Financial and corporate compliance grew just 3% organically in 2025 because United States merger and lending volumes are subdued and Corporate Transparency Act enforcement is suspended. The current regime read describes a record first half for global deal announcements but a July that is digestion rather than fresh supply, alongside a live oil shock and a private-credit gating wave. If corporate activity stalls further, this division stays a drag well into 2027. The offsetting point is that this is cyclical slack rather than secular decay, so it is depressed rather than peak.

Fourth, sector contagion. Because this name moves with RELX, Thomson Reuters and Clarivate on a single shared driver, a bad print from any of them re-prices Wolters Kluwer regardless of its own results. Thomson Reuters reports in early August. That is a risk this position cannot diversify away, and it is the main reason to size it as a single sector expression rather than as an independent idea.

What is notably absent from the risk list: exposure to the two macro factors the current regime read flags as swamping the book. This business has essentially no sensitivity to oil and the Hormuz blockade, and it is not an artificial-intelligence capital-expenditure name, so it does not resolve on the hyperscaler guides. Its driver is genuinely independent of both.
positioning_washout:
The forced selling has largely already happened, and that is a substantial part of why this is actionable now rather than a quarter ago. A fall from 144.25 euros to a low of 54.64 euros is a 62% drawdown in a large, liquid, widely-held European compounder that sat in a great many quality-growth and dividend-growth mandates. A decline of that size in a name of that profile does not occur without mandate-level liquidation: quality-factor and low-volatility strategies mechanically shed a holding whose drawdown and volatility profile has broken, and growth managers cannot defend a position whose structural story is under public attack. The screener's positioning readings corroborate a shareholder base that has been emptied out rather than one still crowded: a smart-money score of 10 out of 100 with institutional flow at a neutral 50 out of 100.

The important structural point is that this is not a dividend-cut or pivot situation, so there is no second mechanical wave waiting. The dividend is progressive and rising (payments up 8% to 563 million euros in 2025), it is covered several times over by guided free cash flow, and management reaffirmed the policy. Yield-focused holders are not being forced out. Equally, the shares are not a crowded short or a heavily-owned momentum name whose unwind is still pending; the unwind is what produced the 54.64 euro low.

On the buy side, the mechanical bid is smaller than it was but is not gone, and it is easy to misread. The 2026 buyback is authorised at up to 500 million euros against 1,096 million euros actually deployed in 2025, which looks like a sharp reduction in support. In share-count terms the gap is much narrower than it appears, because the same euros retire far more stock at 67 euros than at the prices paid in 2025: roughly 3.3% of the current market value versus about 4.3% retired last year. Adding the dividend, total cash returned to shareholders is running near 7% of the market value annually against an 8.9% free-cash-flow yield. Management was also buying through the de-rating, with disclosed repurchase activity in each week of July 2026.

The one genuine negative in the positioning picture is the absence of insider buying. The screener records an insider buy ratio of zero. In a stock down more than half, with a new chief executive who took over during 2026, the absence of a single meaningful personal purchase is a real dog that did not bark, and it argues against sizing this at maximum conviction.

The risk that remains is the reverse of a washout: after a roughly 12.7% three-session rally, some of the buying now is fast money positioning ahead of 5 August, and that money will leave immediately on a soft print.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a buy now, at conviction four, and the reason the call moves up from the prior review's wait-for-the-wash-out is dated evidence rather than a re-reading of the same facts.

The setup is a genuine wide-moat compounder that has been repriced as a melting asset on a thesis that has now been tested twice and failed twice. At 67.36 euros the shares change hands at about 11.9 times last year's reported earnings, 9.8 times cash profit and an 8.9% free-cash-flow yield, against a business that grew organically 6% in each of the last three years, expanded its adjusted operating margin from 26.5% to a guided 28.0%, raised return on invested capital toward a guided 18-19%, and derives 83% of revenue from recurring subscriptions. The prior review set fair value at 82 euros and said to wait for the wash-out. The wash-out came: the shares bottomed at 54.64 euros. And then on 23 July 2026 RELX, the closest comparable business in the world, reported underlying revenue up 7% with growth accelerating in its legal division, reaffirmed its outlook, and triggered a cohort-wide re-rating that has carried this stock up about 12.7% in three sessions. That is a dated fact that did not exist a week ago, and it is the first hard external test of the displacement thesis in the exact division the bears named.

On valuation, the base case is 96 euros per share, built by valuing each division on its disclosed 2025 operating profit against multiples anchored on where the peer group trades today rather than where it used to trade. That distinction matters and is where the supplied peer file had to be overruled: it anchors on RELX and Thomson Reuters at 25-30 times or more, which is simply no longer true, because they were hit by the same shock. Live, RELX is at 21.3 times earnings and Thomson Reuters at 28.4 times against Wolters Kluwer at 11.9 times. The base case of 96 euros still leaves the company at a discount to both peers on every measure, and it sits below the cluster of the screener's own discounted cash flow, Graham and owner-earnings estimates.

The sizing discipline comes from three honest caveats. First, this is sector beta, not single-name alpha. All four names in this cohort moved together again today on one unresolved driver, and a position here is in substance a position on whether generative artificial intelligence eats professional information. It must be sized as one expression of that question, not as an independent idea. Second, a properly adverse sum-of-the-parts, one that cuts the legal division's profit by 45%, still lands at roughly 64 euros, only about 5% below the current price. That is the good news and the bad news together: most of the feared impairment is already in the price, but there is no structural floor beneath it, because net debt is 4.2 billion euros, tangible book is deeply negative and intangibles are about 69% of assets. Third, we are entering nine days before the company's own half-year results on 5 August and immediately after a sharp rally, so the near-term risk of giving back the move is real.

What earns the fourth point of conviction rather than the third is the quality of the residual value case once the event overlay is set aside, which is how this book is now required to judge. The profit pool genuinely exposed to displacement is about a tenth of the total: legal and regulatory, at 183 million euros of operating profit on the lowest margin in the group. The other 90% sits behind a statutory registered-agent requirement, filing infrastructure with spreading electronic-invoicing mandates, and clinical decision support whose entire value is verified accuracy and professional liability. The market has repriced a tenth of the company as though it were the whole of it.

What holds it back from a fifth point is the same thing that holds back the value score: durability is inferred, not confirmed. Management has now been asked for four consecutive quarters to quantify artificial-intelligence revenue, acquisition growth rates and UpToDate retention, and has declined every time. The step-up in product development spending from 11% to 12-13% of revenue is a permanent admission that holding this ground costs more than it did. There has been no insider buying through a 62% drawdown. And the margin sits 1.34 standard deviations above its historical peak, even if the depressed transactional lines argue that the revenue mix underneath it is not peak at all.

On the current regime, the tilt is applied but it does not move the score much in either direction, which is the correct outcome. This thesis depends on no rate cut, so it takes no penalty on that axis. Its resolution driver is genuinely independent of both macro factors the regime read flags as swamping the book: it has no oil or Hormuz sensitivity and it is not an artificial-intelligence capital-expenditure name, so it does not resolve on the hyperscaler guides in late July. In a book being told to enforce resolution-driver independence hard against two correlated factors, that independence is worth something real. The 5 August results date also lands just after the dense 22-30 July event cluster the regime read warns about, in the cleaner early-August window. Under this book's catalyst-neutrality rule the scheduled results date is recorded as description, not credit; the position is underwritten on the value case.

One forensic note that materially affected the arithmetic and should be carried forward: two figures in the supplied metrics are corrupted. Trailing twelve-month diluted earnings per share of 10.12 euros and trailing free cash flow of 3.00 billion euros are two-year sums, an artifact of the data provider treating this semi-annual reporter's half-year filings as quarters. The true figures are 5.64 euros and 1,348 million euros. Valuing off the uncorrected numbers would have made the shares appear roughly twice as cheap as they are and would have produced a fair value near 190 euros. The numbers in this record are built from the company's disclosed divisional accounts instead, and the resulting enterprise value cross-checks to within 1 million euros of the independently reported figure.

interrogator_dossier:
# Wolters Kluwer (WKL.AS) — a deep dive on management and the setup

*Forensic review of four consecutive results calls (July 2024, February 2025, July 2025, February 2026), cross-checked against the reported financials, the Q1 2026 trading update of 6 May 2026, and the live tape of 27 July 2026.*

**Price used throughout: €67.36 per share on the Amsterdam listing (Euronext Amsterdam, ticker WKL), 27 July 2026, up 7.8% on the day.** All figures are in euros unless stated.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

The story management tells has changed in one important way across these four calls, and it is not the way the share price implies.

In mid-2024 the framing was operational. Nancy McKinstry, then chief executive, led with "expert solutions" — the company's label for products that do a professional's work rather than just inform it — and with the completion of a two-year programme to centralise core functions, "now focused on driving scale economies and operational excellence." Generative artificial intelligence appeared as a feature being added to existing platforms: the company had "integrated Gen AI features into a number of our platforms." It was an efficiency story with a technology garnish.

By the February 2026 call the order had reversed. Artificial intelligence is now the organising idea, and the first substantive claim of the call is that "nearly 70% of our digital revenues are from AI-powered solutions." The named products have changed from platforms-with-features to purpose-built tools: UpToDate Expert AI in the health division, CCH Axcess Expert AI in tax and accounting, and Libra in legal. Stacey Caywood, who took over as chief executive during 2026, describes a shift from adding capability to charging for it.

The most telling change is in spending. Product development ran at a steady 11% of revenue through 2024 and 2025. For 2026 the company guides that ratio up to 12-13% "to further advance our AI strategy." Nothing else in the four calls represents as clear an admission that the cost of defending this franchise has risen.

Two threads were quietly dropped or downgraded. The first is the "expert solutions" share metric — 59% of revenue in both mid-2024 and full-year 2024, then reported as growing 6% organically in mid-2025, then essentially absent from the February 2026 highlights in favour of the AI-powered-revenue framing. The same revenue base, relabelled for a new argument. The second is non-recurring revenue, which went from a modest positive contributor to a persistent drag, discussed each call in progressively more defensive terms.

Nothing in the arc suggests a company in retreat. It suggests a company that has recognised the terms of the argument have changed and is spending to fight on the new ground.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

| Management claim | Where said | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Organic growth is durable around 6% | All four calls | 6% (2023), 6% (2024), 6% (2025), 5% in Q1 2026 | Holds, with mild deceleration |
| The margin keeps improving | All four calls | Adjusted operating margin 27.1% (2024) to 27.5% (2025); guided to about 28.0% for 2026 | Holds |
| Returns on capital are rising | All four calls | Return on invested capital 18.1% (2024), 18.5% at mid-2025, 18.0% (2025), guided 18-19% for 2026 | Holds; the 2025 dip is deployment, not decay |
| The balance sheet is strong | All four calls | Net debt to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation went 1.6x, to 2.1x, to 2.0x, to 1.9x at March 2026 | Holds, but leverage stepped up on acquisitions |
| Cash conversion returns to normal | July 2024 | Guided about 95% for 2024, delivered 102%; guided 95-100% for 2025, delivered 103% | Over-delivered twice |
| Recurring revenue is the engine | All four calls | Recurring revenue 82% of the group (2024) rising to 83% (2025); digital and service subscriptions grew a steady 7-8% organically throughout | Holds |
| Acquisitions are performing | Feb 2026 | RASi, Brightflag and Libra described as "performing ahead of initial expectations"; no supporting figures disclosed | Unverifiable |
| Artificial intelligence supports pricing and retention | July 2025, Feb 2026 | No revenue attribution given for two years; first hard adoption numbers appeared only in the Q1 2026 update | Weakly supported until 2026 |

Where the story is **richer than the numbers**: the artificial-intelligence monetisation claim. Management has asserted since mid-2025 that these features "support retention, support price increases," but declined to quantify it. Asked directly by Lisa Yang of Goldman Sachs in July 2025 for "roughly uptick per customer, able to raise prices more," McKinstry answered: "it's early days right now in terms of doing that... we're still working through that." That is the single largest gap between narrative and evidence in the file, and it went unclosed for four consecutive quarters.

Where the story is **poorer than the numbers**: the composition of growth. Management repeatedly apologises for the non-recurring lines — on-premise software licences, implementation fees, transaction volumes and print — without emphasising that these are shrinking precisely because customers are moving to the recurring cloud products the company wants them on. In the first half of 2025, total non-recurring revenue fell 4% while other non-recurring fell 9%; for the full year, other non-recurring fell 5%. Print, now under 5% of revenue, cost the group 50 basis points of organic growth in 2025. The reported 5-6% headline understates the health of the 83% of revenue that actually compounds.

A second point in the company's favour, rarely made by management: the transactional business inside financial and corporate compliance is depressed, not peaking. It grew 2% in 2025 against a backdrop management describes as "continued stagnation in U.S. M&A volumes and corporate lending activity," compounded by the suspended enforcement of the Corporate Transparency Act. That is cyclical slack, and it sits underneath a margin the screener flags as being 1.34 standard deviations above its historical peak. The margin is high; the revenue mix feeding it is not.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: Stable, with a deliberate shift from defensive to offensive between the 2025 and 2026 calls.**

July 2024 — confident and operational. "I'm pleased to say that we had a good start to the year, and we are on track to meet our full year guidance." The emphasis is on centralisation completed and "scale economies," which is the vocabulary of a company harvesting rather than investing.

February 2025 — the most comfortable of the four. "So all in all, a good year." Guidance was met or beaten on every line, and McKinstry closes by introducing her successor warmly. No hedging.

July 2025 — the low point for confidence on growth, the high point on margin. Organic growth is described as "5%, slightly lower than the prior period as we had guided," while the margin jumped 190 basis points. Management is explicitly cautious about the second half: "we'll face currency headwinds, additional restructuring and the absence of last year's EUR 27 million pension gain." That is unusually specific downside framing, offered unprompted.

February 2026 — a change of voice and a change of stance. Caywood is markedly more commercial and more specific than her predecessor on pricing, and she commits capital rather than defending margin: product development goes up to 12-13% of revenue. Asked where the market is moving faster than expected, she does not deflect into reassurance but reports a live observation from her tax leader that "the difference between last year and this year in terms of customer interest and recognition that these solutions can really deliver value has increased a lot."

Guidance specificity **increased** over the period rather than degrading. The 2026 outlook carries a point margin target (about 28.0%), a free-cash-flow range (€1,300-1,350 million), a returns range (18-19%) and a spending commitment — more precision than the ranges given in 2024, which is not the behaviour of a management team bracing for a miss.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: High.**

The record across the four calls is consistent over-delivery on cash and margin, and precise delivery on earnings.

- **2024 margin:** guided to a 26.4-26.8% range in July 2024; delivered 27.1%. Critically, management volunteered that a one-time non-cash pension gain of €27 million contributed roughly 50 basis points and that "excluding this pension gain, our margin would have been within our guidance range." Disclosing the flattering item unprompted, in the same breath as the beat, is a strong credibility marker.
- **2024 cash conversion:** guided to about 95%; delivered 102%.
- **2024 free cash flow:** €1,276 million, up 9% in constant currency and explicitly "ahead of our expectations."
- **2025 margin:** delivered 27.5%, "at the top end of our guidance range."
- **2025 cash conversion:** guided 95-100%; delivered 103%.
- **2025 earnings per share:** diluted adjusted earnings per share of €5.29, up 9% in constant currency, "in line with our guidance, which we raised in July of 2025."
- **2025 free cash flow:** €1,348 million, up 10%, "above our expectation."

This reconciles cleanly with the screener's earnings-beat record of six of the last seven quarters. There is a mild sandbagging pattern on cash conversion — guided to 95-100% twice, delivered above 100% twice — but it is modest and consistently framed as timing.

One caveat worth carrying: the July 2024 call guided capital expenditure "closer to the top end of our range of 5% to 6% of revenues," and the company then came in at 5.3%, blamed on "timing of investments." Under-spending against a stated investment intention is the one place where delivery ran the wrong way, and it is mildly relevant to a company now promising to spend more on product.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Three questions recur and are not fully answered.

**How much money is artificial intelligence actually making?** Lisa Yang of Goldman Sachs pressed hardest in July 2025, asking management to "quantify the benefit you're seeing so far." The answer was a description of process, not a number. The company has since offered adoption statistics — more than half of United States enterprise customers using UpToDate Expert AI, and over 150 accounting firms on the new CCH Axcess agentic modules, both disclosed in the Q1 2026 update — but still no revenue attribution. Until that number exists, neither the bull nor the bear case on this stock can be settled from company disclosure.

**How fast are the acquisitions growing?** Asked directly in July 2025, McKinstry declined: "we don't disclose that, but I would say that all three of them... are growing more than the core, right? That's so higher growth than the core and leave it there." The company spent €896 million on acquisitions in 2025 and roughly €342 million in 2024. Refusing to disclose the growth of nearly €1.25 billion of deployed capital is a real governance gap, and it makes the "performing ahead of initial expectations" claim in February 2026 unverifiable.

**What is UpToDate's retention rate?** In February 2026 an analyst asked precisely, offering his own estimate ("I believe it's low 90s") to make it easy to confirm or correct. Caywood answered with texture — "we signed more multiyear contracts for longer durations with higher annual contract value last year than we had in prior years" — but not the number. That answer is genuinely informative and arguably better than a retention percentage, but it is still a deflection of the specific metric that would most directly test the displacement thesis.

One pressure point that later proved well-founded: Henk Slotboom of The Idea challenged the price paid for the Isabel Group accounting business in July 2024, noting he was "used to seeing you paying five or six times sales and this was somewhere between nine and 10 times sales." Management defended it as market rate for faster-growing software. Acquisition spending then accelerated sharply, and leverage rose from 1.6 times to 2.1 times within a year. The analyst was right to flag a change in capital-allocation posture.

What analysts are **not** yet pressing on, and should: the 2026 share buyback is set at up to €500 million against €1,096 million actually deployed in 2025. Nobody asked why.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- *Non-recurring revenue in persistent decline.* First half 2025 non-recurring revenue fell 4%, with other non-recurring down 9%; full-year 2025 other non-recurring fell 5%. Print books fell 11% across the group and 17% in health in the first half of 2025. Roughly 17% of revenue is shrinking.
- *Acquisition discipline loosened.* Nine to ten times sales for Isabel against a historical five to six times (July 2024 call), €896 million deployed in 2025, leverage from 1.6 to 2.1 times inside twelve months.
- *Two years of refusing to quantify artificial-intelligence monetisation*, plus refusal to disclose acquisition growth rates and UpToDate retention. These are the three numbers that would settle the debate, and none is available.
- *The buyback is smaller in 2026* — up to €500 million versus €1,096 million in 2025 — which removes some of the mechanical support under the shares, though at a much lower share price the same euros retire proportionally more stock.
- *No tangible asset backing.* Intangibles are roughly 69% of total assets and tangible book value is deeply negative, a consequence of decades of acquisitions and buybacks. There is no asset floor beneath this equity.
- *Financial and corporate compliance decelerated to 3% organic in 2025*, hit simultaneously by subdued deal and lending volumes and the suspended enforcement of the Corporate Transparency Act.
- *The 2024 margin beat was flattered* by a €27 million pension gain worth about 50 basis points — disclosed, but it means the underlying 2024 improvement was smaller than the headline.

**Green flags**

- *Every division still grew after the shock.* In the first quarter of 2026 — the first full quarter following Anthropic's 3 February 2026 launch of a legal plug-in for Claude, the event that triggered the sector's de-rating — the group grew 5% organically with health at 5%, tax and accounting at 4%, financial and corporate compliance at 5%, **legal and regulatory at 5%**, and corporate performance and environmental, social and governance at 5%. The division most directly in the line of fire did not decelerate.
- *Guidance was reaffirmed at that same Q1 2026 update*, including the roughly 28.0% margin target and 18-19% returns.
- *Voluntary disclosure of the pension gain* that flattered the 2024 margin.
- *Recurring revenue rose* from 82% to 83% of the group, with the largest component — digital and service subscriptions — compounding at a steady 7-8% organically across all four calls.
- *Cloud software revenue grew 15-16% organically for three consecutive years* and passed on-premise software for the first time in 2024.
- *Returns on capital rose* from 17.5% at mid-2024 to 18.5% at mid-2025, held at 18.0% in 2025 despite €896 million of fresh capital deployed, and are guided to 18-19% for 2026.
- *Artificial intelligence is currently raising prices, not lowering them.* Caywood disclosed in February 2026 that for Libra, the legal workspace product, "the average price is about 2x the value of the content offering that we would sell to a law firm."
- *Cash returns remain large.* Dividends and repurchases together came to €1.7 billion in 2025, more than 120% of free cash flow.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**The relabelling of the same revenue base.** "Expert solutions grew 7% organically and reached 59% of the group's revenues" (February 2025) became "nearly 70% of our digital revenues are from AI-powered solutions" (February 2026). The underlying products barely changed. This is management repositioning an existing franchise inside a narrative it did not choose, which is a rational response to a de-rating but should not be mistaken for new growth.

**The moat argument, stated plainly and correctly.** In February 2025 McKinstry described the technical approach: "we work in what we call small language models, right, where we work only with our proprietary content, and so we have very high accuracy rates." She then added the part that matters most: "we still put editorial resources on top of that, not just in health, but in legal. So, we have a very strong track record with our customers around the accuracy." The defence being offered is not raw model capability — which the company will lose — but verified accuracy and the professional liability that attaches to being wrong. That is the correct place to plant a flag, and it is why health and compliance should prove far more durable than general legal research.

**The new chief executive prices differently.** McKinstry spoke about pricing in general terms. Caywood enumerates the unit of value product by product: firm size plus number of returns for CCH Axcess, institutions for UpToDate enterprise, request lists sent for the client collaboration tool, consumption tiers for the intelligence product. She also distinguishes the older artificial-intelligence features, which were "more about supporting our renewal rates with price increases," from newer ones the company is "discretely monetising." That is a sharper commercial posture and it is the most substantive change the leadership transition has produced.

**Capital-allocation language never drifted.** Kevin Entricken, the chief financial officer, gave the same three priorities — investment in the business, paying down debt, rewarding shareholders — in essentially identical words across the whole period. Consistency here is a mild positive; there is no evidence of a strategy being rewritten under pressure.

**What the spending increase concedes.** Raising product development from 11% to 12-13% of revenue is roughly €60-120 million of additional annual spend. Management frames it as opportunity. It is equally an acknowledgement that the price of holding this ground went up, and it should be treated as a permanent addition to the cost base rather than a one-off investment cycle.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.**

This is a business whose operating performance has been remarkably steady through the most violent share-price de-rating in its modern history. Revenue compounded from €4.77 billion in 2021 to €6.13 billion in 2025; net income from €728 million to €1.31 billion; earnings per share from €2.78 to €5.64. Margins expanded, returns on capital rose, cash conversion beat guidance twice, and the most recent trading update showed every single division still growing. The shares nonetheless trade at €67.36 against a 52-week high of €144.25.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** the entire investment case turns on whether the professional-information franchise is defended by workflow habit or by verified accuracy and regulatory obligation. If it is habit, generative artificial intelligence dissolves it and today's low multiple is a trap. If it is accuracy and obligation, the multiple is a fear-print. The evidence available today favours the second reading — every division grew in the first quarter after the shock, and the closest comparable company reported accelerating legal growth on 23 July 2026 — but management has withheld the three disclosures that would settle it: revenue attributable to artificial-intelligence products, acquisition growth rates, and UpToDate retention. The director is sizing a position on inference, not on confirmation, and should size accordingly.

**Economic moat: WIDE.** The moat is a blend of three types. *Switching costs* in tax and accounting and in corporate performance, where the software is wired into filing calendars, consolidation processes and firm workflows. *Regulatory licence* in financial and corporate compliance, where CT Corporation's registered-agent business exists because every United States entity is legally required to have one — a business essentially untouchable by a language model. *Intangible brand and liability* in health, where UpToDate is cited at the point of clinical decision and the value is precisely that a human editorial process stands behind it.

The width test is the returns and margin evidence, and it points the right way: gross margin stable at 73.5%, adjusted operating margin rising from 26.5% in the first half of 2024 to a guided 28.0% for 2026, and return on invested capital moving from 17.5% to a guided 18-19%. These are expanding, not eroding, economics. This is not a high-but-falling returns profile.

**Moat trend: STABLE.** Margins and returns are improving, which would argue for widening. But the competitive bar has demonstrably risen — the company must now spend 12-13% of revenue rather than 11% to hold position — so the honest reading is that the franchise is holding its ground at a higher cost, not extending it.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal.** Generative artificial intelligence is a real and permanent threat to the parts of this company that sell searchable content. That is essentially the legal and regulatory division: €1,005 million of revenue and €183 million of adjusted operating profit in 2025, which is 16% of group revenue but only 10% of divisional profit, and it already earns the lowest margin in the group at 18.2%. The remaining 90% of segment profit sits behind clinical liability, filing requirements and statutory obligation. A threat that can impair a tenth of the profit pool is material and deserves a lower multiple than the company once carried; it is not a threat to terminal value.

The cheapness is therefore best read as a **fear-print rather than a structurally shrinking base** — with the important qualifier that the fear is directionally rational and the market is right to have removed the old premium. The error is one of degree, not of kind.

A decline of that size in a name of that profile does not occur without mandate-level liquidation: quality-factor and low-volatility strategies mechanically shed a holding whose drawdown and volatility profile has broken, and growth managers cannot defend a position whose structural story is under public attack. The screener's positioning readings corroborate a shareholder base that has been emptied out rather than one still crowded: a smart-money score of 10 out of 100 with institutional flow at a neutral 50 out of 100.

The important structural point is that this is not a dividend-cut or pivot situation, so there is no second mechanical wave waiting. The dividend is progressive and rising (payments up 8% to 563 million euros in 2025), it is covered several times over by guided free cash flow, and management reaffirmed the policy. Yield-focused holders are not being forced out. Equally, the shares are not a crowded short or a heavily-owned momentum name whose unwind is still pending; the unwind is what produced the 54.64 euro low.

On the buy side, the mechanical bid is smaller than it was but is not gone, and it is easy to misread. The 2026 buyback is authorised at up to 500 million euros against 1,096 million euros actually deployed in 2025, which looks like a sharp reduction in support. In share-count terms the gap is much narrower than it appears, because the same euros retire far more stock at 67 euros than at the prices paid in 2025: roughly 3.3% of the current market value versus about 4.3% retired last year. Adding the dividend, total cash returned to shareholders is running near 7% of the market value annually against an 8.9% free-cash-flow yield. Management was also buying through the de-rating, with disclosed repurchase activity in each week of July 2026.

The one genuine negative in the positioning picture is the absence of insider buying. The screener records an insider buy ratio of zero. In a stock down more than half, with a new chief executive who took over during 2026, the absence of a single meaningful personal purchase is a real dog that did not bark, and it argues against sizing this at maximum conviction.

The risk that remains is the reverse of a washout: after a roughly 12.7% three-session rally, some of the buying now is fast money positioning ahead of 5 August, and that money will leave immediately on a soft print.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a buy now, at conviction four, and the reason the call moves up from the prior review's wait-for-the-wash-out is dated evidence rather than a re-reading of the same facts.

The setup is a genuine wide-moat compounder that has been repriced as a melting asset on a thesis that has now been tested twice and failed twice. At 67.36 euros the shares change hands at about 11.9 times last year's reported earnings, 9.8 times cash profit and an 8.9% free-cash-flow yield, against a business that grew organically 6% in each of the last three years, expanded its adjusted operating margin from 26.5% to a guided 28.0%, raised return on invested capital toward a guided 18-19%, and derives 83% of revenue from recurring subscriptions. The prior review set fair value at 82 euros and said to wait for the wash-out. The wash-out came: the shares bottomed at 54.64 euros. And then on 23 July 2026 RELX, the closest comparable business in the world, reported underlying revenue up 7% with growth accelerating in its legal division, reaffirmed its outlook, and triggered a cohort-wide re-rating that has carried this stock up about 12.7% in three sessions. That is a dated fact that did not exist a week ago, and it is the first hard external test of the displacement thesis in the exact division the bears named.

On valuation, the base case is 96 euros per share, built by valuing each division on its disclosed 2025 operating profit against multiples anchored on where the peer group trades today rather than where it used to trade. That distinction matters and is where the supplied peer file had to be overruled: it anchors on RELX and Thomson Reuters at 25-30 times or more, which is simply no longer true, because they were hit by the same shock. Live, RELX is at 21.3 times earnings and Thomson Reuters at 28.4 times against Wolters Kluwer at 11.9 times. The base case of 96 euros still leaves the company at a discount to both peers on every measure, and it sits below the cluster of the screener's own discounted cash flow, Graham and owner-earnings estimates.

The sizing discipline comes from three honest caveats. First, this is sector beta, not single-name alpha. All four names in this cohort moved together again today on one unresolved driver, and a position here is in substance a position on whether generative artificial intelligence eats professional information. It must be sized as one expression of that question, not as an independent idea. Second, a properly adverse sum-of-the-parts, one that cuts the legal division's profit by 45%, still lands at roughly 64 euros, only about 5% below the current price. That is the good news and the bad news together: most of the feared impairment is already in the price, but there is no structural floor beneath it, because net debt is 4.2 billion euros, tangible book is deeply negative and intangibles are about 69% of assets. Third, we are entering nine days before the company's own half-year results on 5 August and immediately after a sharp rally, so the near-term risk of giving back the move is real.

What earns the fourth point of conviction rather than the third is the quality of the residual value case once the event overlay is set aside, which is how this book is now required to judge. The profit pool genuinely exposed to displacement is about a tenth of the total: legal and regulatory, at 183 million euros of operating profit on the lowest margin in the group. The other 90% sits behind a statutory registered-agent requirement, filing infrastructure with spreading electronic-invoicing mandates, and clinical decision support whose entire value is verified accuracy and professional liability. The market has repriced a tenth of the company as though it were the whole of it.

What holds it back from a fifth point is the same thing that holds back the value score: durability is inferred, not confirmed. Management has now been asked for four consecutive quarters to quantify artificial-intelligence revenue, acquisition growth rates and UpToDate retention, and has declined every time. The step-up in product development spending from 11% to 12-13% of revenue is a permanent admission that holding this ground costs more than it did. There has been no insider buying through a 62% drawdown. And the margin sits 1.34 standard deviations above its historical peak, even if the depressed transactional lines argue that the revenue mix underneath it is not peak at all.

On the current regime, the tilt is applied but it does not move the score much in either direction, which is the correct outcome. This thesis depends on no rate cut, so it takes no penalty on that axis. Its resolution driver is genuinely independent of both macro factors the regime read flags as swamping the book: it has no oil or Hormuz sensitivity and it is not an artificial-intelligence capital-expenditure name, so it does not resolve on the hyperscaler guides in late July. In a book being told to enforce resolution-driver independence hard against two correlated factors, that independence is worth something real. The 5 August results date also lands just after the dense 22-30 July event cluster the regime read warns about, in the cleaner early-August window. Under this book's catalyst-neutrality rule the scheduled results date is recorded as description, not credit; the position is underwritten on the value case.

Trailing twelve-month diluted earnings per share of 10.12 euros and trailing free cash flow of 3.00 billion euros are two-year sums, an artifact of the data provider treating this semi-annual reporter's half-year filings as quarters. The true figures are 5.64 euros and 1,348 million euros. Valuing off the uncorrected numbers would have made the shares appear roughly twice as cheap as they are and would have produced a fair value near 190 euros. The numbers in this record are built from the company's disclosed divisional accounts instead, and the resulting enterprise value cross-checks to within 1 million euros of the independently reported figure.
